# The Value of Disagreement

## Why a Good Meeting Doesn't End in Consensus

There's a common intuition about meetings: the best ones end with everyone nodding, aligned, ready to march forward together. We've all felt the satisfaction of a room reaching agreement, the visible relief when a contentious discussion finally settles. But this intuition deserves scrutiny. Agreement, it turns out, can be a mirage. It can mask confusion, unspoken doubts, and fundamental misunderstandings about what was actually decided. A genuinely productive meeting might end not with harmony, but with a precise, honest map of what people disagree about—and a plan for resolving it.

## The Problem with False Consensus

Consider a familiar scenario. A product team meets to decide whether to launch a new feature. The discussion goes well—no one raises objections, the room seems enthusiastic, and the meeting ends with a sense of momentum. Six weeks later, the launch stumbles. In the post-mortem, it emerges that the engineer thought the feature was a prototype to test user interest, the designer believed it was a polished product meant to showcase the company's craft, and the marketing lead assumed it would be promoted heavily. Everyone "agreed" to launch. Nobody agreed on what launch meant
